source.text: Τί οὖν ἐροῦμεν εὑρηκέναι Ἀβραὰμ τὸν προπάτορα ἡμῶν κατὰ σάρκα;

records.literal_gloss: What then will we say to have found Abraham the forefather of us according to flesh?

en.L: What then will we say that Abraham, our forefather according to [the] flesh, has found?
en.B: What then are we to say that Abraham, our ancestor by natural descent, has found?
en.R: Think about Abraham, the ancestor of the Jewish people. What did he find out about being right with God?

decisions.reason: Abraham was honored as the father of the Jewish people. Paul, a Jew, says "our forefather according to the flesh"; from verse 11 he shows that Abraham is father in a wider sense too.

decisions.choice: one question: what did Abraham find?
alternatives: two questions: "What then shall we say? Have we found Abraham to be our forefather according to the flesh?"
decisions.reason: The Greek can also be divided into two questions, asking whether believers, Jew and Gentile, belong to Abraham's family by natural descent. The question about what Abraham found fits verse 2, which asks how he was declared righteous.

decisions.choice: "has found" stands in the text, after "say"
alternatives: some manuscripts put "has found" after "Abraham" or "our forefather"
at least one important early manuscript leaves it out
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT reads "has found" after "what then shall we say". (From general knowledge of the manuscripts; to be checked against the apparatus.)
Readable says what the question is about, which verse 2 makes clear.

source.text: εἰ γὰρ Ἀβραὰμ ἐξ ἔργων ἐδικαιώθη, ἔχει καύχημα· ἀλλ’ οὐ πρὸς θεόν, τί γὰρ ἡ γραφὴ λέγει;

records.literal_gloss: If for Abraham by works was justified, he has a boast; but not toward God. \v 3 What for the Scripture says?

en.L: For if Abraham was justified by works, he has a boast, but not before God. \v 3 For what does the Scripture say?
en.B: Suppose Abraham was declared righteous because of his works: then he would have grounds for boasting, but not in God's presence. \v 3 What does Scripture say?
en.R: If Abraham had been made right with God because of the good things he did, he would have something to be proud of. But he could not be proud in front of God. \v 3 Look at what the Scriptures say:

decisions.reason: Jewish writings of the time held Abraham up as faithful in testing. 1 Maccabees 2:52 asks, "Was not Abraham found faithful when tested, and it was counted to him as righteousness?", linking Genesis 15:6 to the sacrifice of Isaac (Genesis 22). Paul goes back to Genesis 15 itself.

decisions.choice: but not before God: he has no boast where it counts
alternatives: he could boast before people but not before God
decisions.reason: Paul grants the "if" for the sake of argument, then denies it where it matters: before God Abraham has nothing to boast of, as Scripture shows.

decisions.choice: declared righteous / made right with God
decisions.reason: As in 2:13 and 3:24.

source.text: Ἐπίστευσεν δὲ Ἀβραὰμ τῷ θεῷ καὶ ἐλογίσθη αὐτῷ εἰς δικαιοσύνην.

records.literal_gloss: Believed and Abraham the God, and it was counted to him for righteousness.

en.L: "And Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness."
en.B: "Abraham believed God, and that was counted to him as righteousness."
en.R: "Abraham believed God, and God counted that as righteousness."

decisions.reason: The quotation is Genesis 15:6, in the wording of the Greek translation. In Genesis it follows God's promise that Abraham's offspring would be as many as the stars. Paul quotes it again in Galatians 3:6.
λογίζομαι is a bookkeeping word: to put something to someone's account. Verse 4 uses it of wages. God put righteousness to Abraham's account when he believed.
λογίζομαι comes eleven times in this chapter. The same English is kept wherever it can be, so that the thread of Paul's argument stays visible, as in 9:8.
Readable names God as the one who counts.

source.text: τῷ δὲ ἐργαζομένῳ ὁ μισθὸς οὐ λογίζεται κατὰ χάριν ἀλλὰ κατὰ ὀφείλημα·

records.literal_gloss: To the [one] but working the wage not is counted according to grace but according to debt;

en.L: Now to the one who works, the wage is not counted as a matter of grace but as a debt;
en.B: A worker's wages are not counted as grace but as what is owed.
en.R: When people work, their pay is not a gift of grace. It is what they have earned.

decisions.reason: μισθός is pay for work; ὀφείλημα is what is owed. A worker's pay is the employer's obligation, not a favor.
Grace here is a gift given freely, the opposite of what is owed.
λογίζομαι comes eleven times in this chapter. The same English is kept wherever it can be, so that the thread of Paul's argument stays visible, as in 9:8.

source.text: τῷ δὲ μὴ ἐργαζομένῳ, πιστεύοντι δὲ ἐπὶ τὸν δικαιοῦντα τὸν ἀσεβῆ, λογίζεται ἡ πίστις αὐτοῦ εἰς δικαιοσύνην, καθάπερ καὶ Δαυὶδ λέγει τὸν μακαρισμὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ᾧ ὁ θεὸς λογίζεται δικαιοσύνην χωρὶς ἔργων·

records.literal_gloss: to the [one] but not working, believing but on the [one] justifying the ungodly, is counted the faith of him for righteousness, \v 6 just as also David speaks the blessedness of the man to whom the God counts righteousness apart from works;

en.L: but to the one who does not work but believes in the one who justifies the ungodly, {{gender:their|his}} faith is counted as righteousness, \v 6 just as David also speaks of the blessedness of the {{gender:person|man}} to whom God counts righteousness apart from works:
en.B: But to someone who does no work, yet believes in the God who declares the ungodly righteous, that faith is counted as righteousness. \v 6 David says the same when he speaks of the happiness of the one whom God counts as righteous apart from works:
en.R: But some people do not work to earn it. They simply believe in God, who makes ungodly people right with {{deity_pronoun:himself|Himself}}. God counts their faith as righteousness. \v 6 David said the same thing. He talked about how happy people are when God counts them as righteous without their doing anything to earn it.

decisions.reason: The law forbade judges to acquit the guilty (Exodus 23:7, Proverbs 17:15). Paul says that God does declare the ungodly righteous, and 3:25-26 has shown how he can do so and still be just.
μακαρισμός is a pronouncement that someone is blessed, as the psalm does in the next verses.

decisions.choice: David: the psalm is headed "Of David"
decisions.reason: Psalm 32, quoted next, bears David's name in its heading.
The words mean any person who believes, man or woman.

decisions.choice: the God who declares the ungodly righteous
alternatives: the one who justifies the ungodly
decisions.reason: Balanced names God, who is meant.
λογίζομαι comes eleven times in this chapter. The same English is kept wherever it can be, so that the thread of Paul's argument stays visible, as in 9:8.

source.text: Μακάριοι ὧν ἀφέθησαν αἱ ἀνομίαι καὶ ὧν ἐπεκαλύφθησαν αἱ ἁμαρτίαι, μακάριος ἀνὴρ οὗ οὐ μὴ λογίσηται κύριος ἁμαρτίαν.

records.literal_gloss: Blessed [are those] whose were forgiven the lawless deeds and whose were covered the sins; \v 8 blessed man of whom not not will count Lord sin.

en.L: "Blessed [are those] whose lawless deeds were forgiven and whose sins were covered; \v 8 blessed [is the] {{gender:person|man}} whose sin [the] Lord will never count."
en.B: "How happy are those whose wrongs are forgiven, whose sins are covered over! \v 8 How happy is the one whose sin the Lord will never count against them!"
en.R: "How happy are the people whose wrongs God has forgiven, whose sins {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has covered! \v 8 How happy is the person whose sin the Lord will never hold against them!"

decisions.reason: The quotation is Psalm 32:1-2, in the wording of the Greek translation. Where the Greek has "Lord", the Hebrew has God's name, YHWH. The psalm uses the same verb, "count", as Genesis 15:6.
Sins covered are sins God no longer looks on to judge, the language of atonement.
οὐ μὴ together is the strongest denial Greek has.
The word means happy, fortunate, in God's favor. Literal keeps "blessed".
The psalm speaks of anyone, man or woman.
Readable uses the plainest English for counting a sin against someone.

source.text: Ὁ μακαρισμὸς οὖν οὗτος ἐπὶ τὴν περιτομὴν ἢ καὶ ἐπὶ τὴν ἀκροβυστίαν;

records.literal_gloss: The blessedness then this on the circumcision or also on the uncircumcision?

en.L: Is this blessedness then [pronounced] on the circumcised, or also on the uncircumcised?
en.B: Is this blessing, then, only for the circumcised, or also for the uncircumcised?
en.R: Is this happiness only for Jews, who are circumcised? Or is it also for people who are not circumcised?

decisions.choice: the circumcised and the uncircumcised: Jews and Gentiles
decisions.reason: As in 3:30.

source.text: λέγομεν γάρ· Ἐλογίσθη τῷ Ἀβραὰμ ἡ πίστις εἰς δικαιοσύνην.

records.literal_gloss: We say for: was counted to the Abraham the faith for righteousness.

en.L: For we say, "Faith was counted to Abraham as righteousness."
en.B: We have been saying that Abraham's faith was counted to him as righteousness.
en.R: We have said that God counted Abraham's faith as righteousness.

decisions.reason: λογίζομαι comes eleven times in this chapter. The same English is kept wherever it can be, so that the thread of Paul's argument stays visible, as in 9:8.

source.text: πῶς οὖν ἐλογίσθη;

records.literal_gloss: How then was it counted?

en.L: How then was it counted?
en.B: Under what circumstances, then, was it counted?
en.R: When did God count it?

source.text: ἐν περιτομῇ ὄντι ἢ ἐν ἀκροβυστίᾳ;

records.literal_gloss: In circumcision being or in uncircumcision?

en.L: When he was in circumcision or in uncircumcision?
en.B: Was it after he was circumcised, or before?
en.R: Was it after Abraham was circumcised, or before?

source.text: οὐκ ἐν περιτομῇ ἀλλ’ ἐν ἀκροβυστίᾳ·

records.literal_gloss: Not in circumcision but in uncircumcision;

en.L: Not in circumcision but in uncircumcision;
en.B: It was not after, but before.
en.R: It was before he was circumcised.

decisions.reason: Abraham's faith is counted as righteousness in Genesis 15:6; he is circumcised in Genesis 17. Ishmael's birth falls between: Abraham was 86 then and 99 when he was circumcised (Genesis 16:16, 17:24).

source.text: καὶ σημεῖον ἔλαβεν περιτομῆς, σφραγῖδα τῆς δικαιοσύνης τῆς πίστεως τῆς ἐν τῇ ἀκροβυστίᾳ, εἰς τὸ εἶναι αὐτὸν πατέρα πάντων τῶν πιστευόντων δι’ ἀκροβυστίας, εἰς τὸ λογισθῆναι αὐτοῖς τὴν δικαιοσύνην, καὶ πατέρα περιτομῆς τοῖς οὐκ ἐκ περιτομῆς μόνον ἀλλὰ καὶ τοῖς στοιχοῦσιν τοῖς ἴχνεσιν τῆς ἐν ἀκροβυστίᾳ πίστεως τοῦ πατρὸς ἡμῶν Ἀβραάμ.

records.literal_gloss: And sign he received of circumcision, seal of the righteousness of the faith the [one] in the uncircumcision, for the to be him father of all the [ones] believing through uncircumcision, for the to be counted to them the righteousness, \v 12 and father of circumcision to those not from circumcision only but also to those walking in the steps of the in uncircumcision faith of the father of us Abraham.

en.L: And he received [the] sign of circumcision as a seal of the righteousness of the faith [that he had] while uncircumcised, so that he would be [the] father of all who believe while uncircumcised, so that righteousness would be counted to them, \v 12 and [the] father of [the] circumcised, to those who are not only of [the] circumcision but who also walk in the steps of the faith that our father Abraham had while uncircumcised.
en.B: Circumcision was given to him afterward as a sign, a seal on the righteousness that was already his by faith before he was circumcised. In this way he is father to everyone who believes without being circumcised, so that righteousness is counted to them. \v 12 And he is father to the circumcised as well: not to those who are merely circumcised, but to those who walk the same road of faith our father Abraham walked while still uncircumcised.
en.R: Later God gave Abraham circumcision as a sign. It was like a seal to show that God had already counted him as righteous because of his faith, before he was circumcised. So Abraham is the father of everyone who believes, even if they are not circumcised. God counts them as righteous. \v 12 Abraham is also the father of people who are circumcised. But it is not only because they are circumcised. They must also live by faith, as our father Abraham did before he was circumcised.

decisions.reason: Genesis 17:11 calls circumcision "the sign of the covenant". A seal confirms that a document is genuine; circumcision confirmed a righteousness Abraham already had.

decisions.choice: one group: circumcised people who also share Abraham's faith
alternatives: two groups: the circumcised, and those who follow Abraham's faith
decisions.reason: The Greek repeats the article before "walk", which could suggest two groups, but the sense requires one: Abraham is father to Jews who are circumcised and also believe.

decisions.choice: "so that righteousness would be counted to them"
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT has no "also" here. (From general knowledge of the manuscripts; to be checked against the apparatus.)

decisions.choice: walk in the steps: follow the example
decisions.reason: στοιχέω is to walk in line, keep in step; Abraham went ahead, and others follow the path he took.
λογίζομαι comes eleven times in this chapter. The same English is kept wherever it can be, so that the thread of Paul's argument stays visible, as in 9:8.
Readable says who gave the sign and when.

source.text: Οὐ γὰρ διὰ νόμου ἡ ἐπαγγελία τῷ Ἀβραὰμ ἢ τῷ σπέρματι αὐτοῦ, τὸ κληρονόμον αὐτὸν εἶναι κόσμου, ἀλλὰ διὰ δικαιοσύνης πίστεως·

records.literal_gloss: Not for through law the promise to the Abraham or to the seed of him, the heir him to be of world, but through righteousness of faith;

en.L: For the promise to Abraham or to his seed, that he would be heir of [the] world, [was] not through [the] law but through [the] righteousness of faith;
en.B: The promise that he would inherit the world did not come to Abraham or to his offspring through the law, but through the righteousness of faith.
en.R: God promised Abraham and his descendants that the whole world would belong to them. God did not make this promise because Abraham obeyed the law. God made it because of Abraham's faith, which God counted as righteousness.

decisions.reason: God promised Abraham the land (Genesis 12:7, 15:18) and blessing for all the families of the earth through him (Genesis 12:3, 22:17-18). Jewish writings of the time already widened the promise to the whole earth (Sirach 44:21). Paul speaks of the world as the inheritance.

decisions.choice: through the law / through the righteousness of faith
decisions.reason: The promise came long before the law was given at Sinai (Galatians 3:17 counts 430 years). It rested on the righteousness God counted to Abraham's faith.
As in 9:7: the same word at each level throughout Romans.

source.text: εἰ γὰρ οἱ ἐκ νόμου κληρονόμοι, κεκένωται ἡ πίστις καὶ κατήργηται ἡ ἐπαγγελία·

records.literal_gloss: If for those from law heirs, has been emptied the faith and has been nullified the promise;

en.L: For if those who are of [the] law [are] heirs, faith has been emptied and the promise nullified;
en.B: If the heirs are those who rely on the law, faith is made empty and the promise is worthless.
en.R: If people get what God promised by obeying the law, then faith means nothing, and God's promise is worthless.

decisions.choice: those of the law: those whose claim rests on the law
decisions.reason: "Of the law" describes people whose standing comes from the law. If the inheritance depended on that, a promise received by faith would mean nothing.

source.text: ὁ γὰρ νόμος ὀργὴν κατεργάζεται, οὗ δὲ οὐκ ἔστιν νόμος, οὐδὲ παράβασις.

records.literal_gloss: The for law wrath brings about; where but not is law, neither transgression.

en.L: For the law brings about wrath; but where there is no law, neither [is there] transgression.
en.B: The law brings about wrath. But where there is no law, there is no breaking of the law either.
en.R: The law brings God's anger, because people break it. But where there is no law, no one can break it.

decisions.reason: As in 1:18 and 2:5, the wrath is God's judgment on wrongdoing.
As in 2:23. Without a law there is still sin (5:13), but not the breaking of a command.
Readable says how the law brings wrath, as the second half of the verse implies.
As in 1:18.

source.text: Διὰ τοῦτο ἐκ πίστεως, ἵνα κατὰ χάριν, εἰς τὸ εἶναι βεβαίαν τὴν ἐπαγγελίαν παντὶ τῷ σπέρματι, οὐ τῷ ἐκ τοῦ νόμου μόνον ἀλλὰ καὶ τῷ ἐκ πίστεως Ἀβραάμ ὅς ἐστιν πατὴρ πάντων ἡμῶν, καθὼς γέγραπται ὅτι Πατέρα πολλῶν ἐθνῶν τέθεικά σε, κατέναντι οὗ ἐπίστευσεν θεοῦ τοῦ ζῳοποιοῦντος τοὺς νεκροὺς καὶ καλοῦντος τὰ μὴ ὄντα ὡς ὄντα·

records.literal_gloss: Because of this from faith, that according to grace, for the to be firm the promise to all the seed, not to the [one] from the law only but also to the [one] from faith of Abraham, who is father of all of us, \v 17 as it has been written that: Father of many nations I have made you, before whom he believed God the [one] giving life to the dead and calling the [things] not being as being;

en.L: For this reason [it is] by faith, so that [it may be] by grace, so that the promise may be sure to all the seed, not only to the [seed] of the law but also to the [seed] of the faith of Abraham, who is [the] father of us all, \v 17 as it is written, "I have made you [the] father of many nations," before the God whom he believed, who gives life to the dead and calls the things that do not exist as existing;
en.B: So the promise comes through faith, in order that it may rest on grace and stand firm for every one of Abraham's offspring: not only for those who belong to the law, but also for those who belong to the faith of Abraham, the father of all of us. \v 17 Scripture says, "I have made you father of many nations." Before God he is our father, the God he believed, who brings the dead to life and calls into being things that do not exist.
en.R: That is why God's promise comes through faith. It is God's gift of grace, and so it is sure for all of Abraham's descendants. It is not only for those who have the law. It is also for those who have faith as Abraham did. He is the father of all of us who believe. \v 17 As the Scriptures say, God told him, "I have made you the father of many nations." Abraham is our father in the sight of God, the God he believed. God gives life to the dead. He speaks, and things that did not exist come into being.

decisions.reason: "I have made you the father of many nations" is Genesis 17:5, where God changes Abram's name to Abraham.

decisions.choice: the seed of the law and the seed of faith
decisions.reason: Both groups are believers: Jewish believers, who have the law, and Gentile believers, who share Abraham's faith without it. Verse 14 has already ruled out the law alone as the ground of inheritance.

decisions.choice: calls into being what does not exist
alternatives: speaks of what does not yet exist as though it did
decisions.reason: The phrase can describe God's creating word, as in creation, or his naming of what is still to come, as he named Abraham father of nations before he had a son. Paired with "gives life to the dead", it most likely speaks of God's power to create.

decisions.choice: before the God whom he believed
decisions.reason: The Greek is compressed: "before whom he believed, God". Abraham is father of all believers in God's sight, whatever his descent.
As in verse 13.

source.text: ὃς παρ’ ἐλπίδα ἐπ’ ἐλπίδι ἐπίστευσεν εἰς τὸ γενέσθαι αὐτὸν πατέρα πολλῶν ἐθνῶν κατὰ τὸ εἰρημένον· Οὕτως ἔσται τὸ σπέρμα σου·

records.literal_gloss: Who against hope on hope believed for the to become him father of many nations according to the having been spoken: So will be the seed of you;

en.L: who against hope believed in hope, so that he became [the] father of many nations, according to what had been spoken, "So will your seed be";
en.B: Hoping when there was no ground for hope, Abraham believed, and so he became the father of many nations, as God had said to him, "That is how many your offspring will be."
en.R: There was no reason to hope, but Abraham hoped and believed. And so he became the father of many nations, as God had told him: "Your descendants will be as many as the stars."

decisions.reason: God took Abraham outside, told him to count the stars, and said, "So will your offspring be" (Genesis 15:5).
A play on words: when all human reason for hope was gone, Abraham hoped in God.

decisions.choice: so that he became: the result, and God's purpose
decisions.reason: The construction gives the outcome of his believing, which was also what God intended.
Readable includes the stars from Genesis 15:5, since "so" means "as many as the stars".

source.text: καὶ μὴ ἀσθενήσας τῇ πίστει κατενόησεν τὸ ἑαυτοῦ σῶμα νενεκρωμένον, ἑκατονταετής που ὑπάρχων, καὶ τὴν νέκρωσιν τῆς μήτρας Σάρρας, εἰς δὲ τὴν ἐπαγγελίαν τοῦ θεοῦ οὐ διεκρίθη τῇ ἀπιστίᾳ ἀλλὰ ἐνεδυναμώθη τῇ πίστει, δοὺς δόξαν τῷ θεῷ καὶ πληροφορηθεὶς ὅτι ὃ ἐπήγγελται δυνατός ἐστιν καὶ ποιῆσαι.

records.literal_gloss: And not having weakened in the faith he considered the of himself body having been made dead, a hundred years old about being, and the deadness of the womb of Sarah, \v 20 at but the promise of the God not he doubted in the unbelief but was strengthened in the faith, having given glory to the God \v 21 and having been fully convinced that what he has promised able he is also to do.

en.L: And without weakening in faith he considered his own body, already as good as dead (since he was about a hundred years old), and the deadness of Sarah's womb; \v 20 yet with respect to the promise of God he did not waver in unbelief, but was strengthened in faith, giving glory to God, \v 21 and being fully convinced that what {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} had promised {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was able also to do.
en.B: His faith did not weaken when he looked at his own body, as good as dead now that he was about a hundred years old, or at the deadness of Sarah's womb. \v 20 He did not doubt God's promise or waver in unbelief. Instead he grew strong in faith and gave glory to God, \v 21 fully convinced that God had the power to carry out what {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} had promised.
en.R: Abraham was about a hundred years old, and his body was as good as dead. His wife Sarah was too old to have children. Abraham knew this, but his faith did not become weak. \v 20 He did not stop believing God's promise. Instead, his faith grew stronger, and he gave glory to God. \v 21 He was completely sure that God could do what {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} had promised.

alternatives: many manuscripts read "he did not consider his own body"
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts add "not". In the SBLGNT text Abraham faces the facts and believes anyway; in the other reading he does not dwell on them. (From general knowledge of the manuscripts; to be checked against the apparatus.)
διακρίνω here is to be torn between belief and unbelief.
Abraham did what humanity failed to do in 1:21: he gave God glory and trusted his power.

decisions.choice: Paul looks at Abraham's faith as a whole
decisions.reason: Genesis records that Abraham laughed at the promise (Genesis 17:17). Paul speaks of the faith that held through it, which God counted as righteousness.

decisions.choice: Sarah was too old to have children
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly what the phrase means.

source.text: διὸ ἐλογίσθη αὐτῷ εἰς δικαιοσύνην.

records.literal_gloss: Therefore it was counted to him for righteousness.

en.L: Therefore "it was counted to him as righteousness."
en.B: That is why "it was counted to him as righteousness."
en.R: That is why God counted his faith as righteousness.

decisions.reason: Paul repeats the words of Genesis 15:6 from verse 3.
λογίζομαι comes eleven times in this chapter. The same English is kept wherever it can be, so that the thread of Paul's argument stays visible, as in 9:8.

source.text: Οὐκ ἐγράφη δὲ δι’ αὐτὸν μόνον ὅτι ἐλογίσθη αὐτῷ, ἀλλὰ καὶ δι’ ἡμᾶς οἷς μέλλει λογίζεσθαι, τοῖς πιστεύουσιν ἐπὶ τὸν ἐγείραντα Ἰησοῦν τὸν κύριον ἡμῶν ἐκ νεκρῶν, ὃς παρεδόθη διὰ τὰ παραπτώματα ἡμῶν καὶ ἠγέρθη διὰ τὴν δικαίωσιν ἡμῶν.

records.literal_gloss: Not was written but because of him only that it was counted to him, \v 24 but also because of us, to whom it is about to be counted, to those believing on the [one] having raised Jesus the Lord of us from dead, \v 25 who was handed over because of the trespasses of us and was raised because of the justification of us.

en.L: Now it was not written for his sake alone that it was counted to him, \v 24 but also for our sake, to whom it will be counted, who believe in the one who raised Jesus our Lord from [the] dead, \v 25 who was handed over for our trespasses and was raised for our justification.
en.B: The words "it was counted to him" were not written for Abraham alone, \v 24 but for us as well. It will be counted to us who believe in the God who raised Jesus our Lord from the dead. \v 25 Jesus was handed over to die because of our trespasses, and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was raised so that we would be declared righteous.
en.R: The words "God counted it to him" were not written only for Abraham. \v 24 They were also written for us. God will count us as righteous too, all of us who believe in the God who raised Jesus our Lord from death. \v 25 Jesus was handed over to die because of our sins. And God raised {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} to life to make us right with {{deity_pronoun:himself|Himself}}.

decisions.reason: "Handed over because of our trespasses" echoes the Greek translation of Isaiah 53:12, where the servant of the LORD "was handed over because of their sins".

decisions.choice: because of our trespasses; for our justification
decisions.reason: The same preposition is used twice. The first looks back (our trespasses were the reason he was handed over); the second looks forward (he was raised to bring about our being declared righteous).
The verb looks forward: righteousness is counted to everyone who believes, and will be confirmed at the judgment.
The passive leaves God as the one who handed him over, as 8:32 says, using the same verb as 1:24.
λογίζομαι comes eleven times in this chapter. The same English is kept wherever it can be, so that the thread of Paul's argument stays visible, as in 9:8.
Balanced and Readable say what he was handed over to.
